paragraphs: A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and that asylum seekers should be put in "concentration camps", according to the Guardian's account of an ITV undercover investigation. The activist has yet to be publicly identified. The footage is due to be broadcast on Sunday.

He described himself as "pretty hardline about Islam" and said "you cannot be a Muslim and British". On people crossing the Channel in small boats, he said: "In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you're in there."

The recording is part of a wider ITV investigation. Excerpts released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates using racist language. On Friday, Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after ITV showed him making racist comments about Asian homeowners. He said there was "no excuse for my comments".

Reform said it had opened investigations where members had "clearly behaved inappropriately" and that there was "no room for racism" in the party. It told ITV it had improved its vetting, but "one cannot vet a future comment", and that it would not comment on individual cases while investigations continue. Nigel Farage said similarly that "you can't vet people for what they say in the future".

Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said Farage's response showed he was "completely unfit to lead" and that the problems went "right to the top of Reform UK". Farage's reply to that criticism was not included in the Guardian's report.

Anthropic's workforce and the work it does have changed significantly over the past year, according to a report the AI company published on Friday. The company argues its own workplace trends could indicate "how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy", since it has "thoroughly molded its workflows around AI".

The report shows fewer junior hires. The share of junior-level employees in technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025, while the share of junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9%. Technical teams also make up a smaller part of the whole workforce, down from 61% to 56%. Anthropic attributes that to the natural expansion of business functions as it scales and to coding tools that let non-technical employees build software themselves.

Employees describe a fast-paced environment. One was reported as describing an "eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything". In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude, and 20% said their job had shifted "from actually doing work to managing Claudes". The report suggests "human attention and judgement" are becoming a bottleneck as Claude produces a "deluge" of text.

Anthropic says AI adoption has raised productivity, citing more code per person, more sales closed per rep and more contracts processed. It acknowledges that "more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact", but says it has found no sign that code quality is declining.

Meeting time per employee is up 20% from a year ago, and up 16% for technical contributors, based on calendar data. The company links this to the importance of "human trust and accountability", with employees describing face-to-face coordination as indispensable.

Wearing noise-cancelling ear defenders during surgery reduced nausea and vomiting afterward, according to results presented at the Anesthesiology conference in San Diego and reported by New Scientist. Such symptoms are common side effects of anaesthetics, and patients are routinely given drugs to prevent them.

Huayue Liu at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in Suzhou, China, and colleagues recruited 192 patients having keyhole gynaecological surgery under general anaesthesia. Half were randomly assigned noise-blocking ear defenders, worn from the start of anaesthesia until the end of surgery. All patients received standard anaesthesia and anti-nausea medication.

Within 48 hours of surgery, 35 per cent of those wearing ear defenders had nausea or vomiting, compared with 52 per cent of those without. Symptoms were also less severe among the protected group, meaning less vomiting and less effect on daily life. Liu recorded average operating theatre noise of 66 decibels, around the level of a normal conversation.

The reason is unclear. The report says noise is thought to trigger a stress response that activates the autonomic nervous system, which interacts with brainstem pathways involved in nausea and vomiting. Liu stressed that the team did not study the mechanism, so this idea "remains a hypothesis".

Vigi Katlowitz at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston called the data "really encouraging" and in line with research showing anaesthesia "is not simply an off switch". Liu said general anaesthesia produces unconsciousness without necessarily eliminating all neural processing of sound. He hopes to run a larger, multi-site trial measuring noise exposure against nervous system activity in patients under general anaesthetic.

Berkshire Hathaway has invested more than $900 million in Bending Spoons, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday, CNBC reports. The Milan-based holding company listed on the Nasdaq in July and owns older internet names including AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Its stock rose 41% on the news, though some of the gain was lost later in the week, leaving a market value of about $30 billion. It closed Friday at $47.07, against an IPO price of $29.
Bending Spoons describes Berkshire as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy. Analysts at Mizuho called the investment "another vote of confidence" in the company's model.

The company is buying software firms hurt by the rise of AI. In August it agreed to buy Airtable for about $1.3 billion, almost 90% below its late-2021 peak valuation. Last month it agreed to buy Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion. The flip side is job cuts: Bending Spoons said a "large portion" of Airtable's pre-acquisition team would leave with "substantial separation packages", and layoffs have previously hit Evernote, Vimeo and WeTransfer.

CNBC contrasts the approach with private equity firms such as Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners, which typically aimed to cut costs and later sell or list their purchases. Bending Spoons says it wants to generate profits from what it buys rather than seek exits, while taking a hands-on role in products and staffing. Mizuho analyst Lloyd Walmsley said few rivals match its willingness to make substantial product changes.
Customers can feel the effects. After buying Evernote, Bending Spoons raised the annual personal subscription price from $70 to $130 in April 2023.

Mercedes-AMG has revealed the 2028 AMG GT SUV, an electric model that The Verge says is the first time in the brand's 59-year history it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. It is scheduled to reach the US next summer, and official pricing has not been released.

It will come in three trims: GT 53, GT 55 and the flagship GT 63. The top model produces 1,153 horsepower from three axial flux motors, the same setup as the AMG GT four-door coupe. The Verge notes that figure beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control.

The 800-volt architecture supports charging up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery used in the GT 63 and GT 55, and 600kW on the 106kWh battery in the GT 53. Mercedes says 10 to 80 percent takes 12 minutes, and 10 minutes adds up to about 280 miles of WLTP range. Estimated maximum range for the larger battery is 435 miles. The GT 63 weighs 5,941 pounds, close to the Cayenne Turbo Electric at 5,960 and lighter than the Lucid Gravity at 6,100.

For handling, AMG replaced mechanical roll bars with active hydraulic suspension elements meant to reduce pitch and roll. It also uses three-stage air springs and standard rear-axle steering. To keep the AMG character, the car plays recorded sounds of real AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines, simulates gear shifts through paddles and adds seat vibrations.

Inside is a 14-inch display running the MB.OS platform with AI assistants from ChatGPT, Microsoft and Google. A Predictive Performance Manager uses track-mapping data to adjust motor output, which Mercedes says should give more consistent lap times by avoiding battery overheating.

Police in France arrested more than 400 people on Saturday as protests over school conditions and the cost of living turned violent in several cities, according to The Guardian and the BBC. The BBC cited an estimated 550,000 people on the streets. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said most of those arrested were adults who were not part of the high school protests. He said 60 law enforcement officers were injured, including two taken to hospital unconscious.

In Paris, a largely peaceful march turned violent into the evening. Police used teargas and water cannon, and shops were looted. The BBC reported that a town hall fire in Limoges caused part of the roof to collapse and that Lyon's tourist office was burned. Protesters stormed the town hall in Marseille. The mayor of Saint-Étienne said a young man had his hand blown off by a grenade.

The protests began last month at schools in poor northern suburbs of Paris, over teacher absences and run-down buildings. They have since widened to include unions such as the CGT and groups angry over prices. The BBC said Education Minister Édouard Geffray promised 3,000 extra supply teachers on 8 October, but the protests have continued.

Officials and politicians disagreed over who is responsible. Nuñez said the demonstration was hijacked by what he called opportunistic delinquents and ruled out a state of emergency. Authorities blamed the "ultra-left". President Emmanuel Macron said those who attacked prefectures, businesses and town halls would be prosecuted. Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused police of "unleashing" on protesters while condemning looting and arson. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called his comments "dangerous and cynical". Marine Le Pen said protesters' "legitimate demands" had been "held hostage by the far left".
The unrest comes ahead of April's presidential election, and Macron leaves office next year. The Guardian reported that more arrests are expected.

Police in Albania fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in Tirana on Saturday, the fifth consecutive day of clashes, according to Al Jazeera and the BBC. National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference, saying they were deployed "in a limited manner". AFP reported it was the first time they had been used since the demonstrations began.

Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at riot police defending the education ministry and, later, near Prime Minister Edi Rama's office. Police answered with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges. Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days and 132 officers injured. Seven officers were suspended pending investigations into allegations that they exceeded their authority. The health ministry said nine protesters and four officers were treated on Saturday. Local media reported damage and burning barricades in the coastal city of Durres.

Students cite expensive university fees, poor facilities, limited jobs and alleged government corruption. The protests follow months of rallies by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development linked to a company founded by Jared Kushner. A 19-year-old protester told the BBC the movement had been peaceful for 135 days and was now using violence. A 17-year-old student alleged that provocateurs were smashing shops to discredit the demonstrations.

Rama, in power for 13 years, has refused to resign. He blamed the opposition Democratic Party and unnamed "foreign actors" for the unrest. He promised to protect students' right to protest while warning against destruction. The BBC reported that special prosecutors recently arrested the secret service chief, Vlora Hyseni, in a case involving a businessman who is a friend of Rama. Rama says he knows the man but denies knowing of any illegal dealings. His party holds 83 of 140 parliamentary seats, and elections are not due until 2029.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of European diplomats in the occupied West Bank village of Taybeh, near Ramallah, on Saturday, according to the BBC and The Guardian. The group included Belgium's consul general and French, Polish and Catholic Church representatives. Belgium said a consulate car had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. The mayor, Bernard Baudoux, told AFP settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars.

The diplomats had gone to assess the situation after near daily settler attacks on Palestinians harvesting olives. The Palestinian health ministry says at least four people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month, according to The Guardian. A day earlier, Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, were injured in a separate settler assault.

Israeli officials responded in different ways. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar condemned violence by "Israeli rioters" but said it was unfortunate the visit had not been coordinated with the army. The army called it a "severe act of violence", said no soldiers were present and said it was investigating. Police opened an investigation. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office urged caution, saying social media images "do not establish the complete sequence of events". It also cited concerns about a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel" during the olive harvest.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said Israel, as the occupying power, must protect Palestinians and diplomats and bring those responsible to justice. He said Belgium would keep pressing for EU sanctions against those responsible and those who support them. The Guardian noted the attacks came less than two weeks before closely contested Israeli elections.

At least 17 people were killed and 25 injured in a crush at a Durga Puja event in north Kolkata, in West Bengal state, on Saturday, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead and that six of the victims had been identified.

Police said the injured were taken to hospital from a pandal, a temporary pavilion housing idols of the goddess Durga. A police statement attributed the stampede to heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall. A senior police official told AFP that an announcement caused "commotion" once the rain started, and that the crowd waiting outside the pavilion pushed and rushed forward and fell, leading to the stampede. Witnesses told the BBC the rain prompted people to surge toward shelter.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the incident saddening, offered condolences and said the West Bengal government was helping affected families. Al Jazeera reported that his office announced compensation of 200,000 rupees for the families of those who died and 50,000 rupees for each injured person. Interior Minister Amit Shah said the administration was making sure medical facilities were provided to the injured.

Both outlets noted that deadly crowd incidents are not uncommon in India, often blamed on poor management and safety lapses. Al Jazeera listed several recent examples: 30 deaths at the Kumbh Mela last year, 11 fans crushed at cricket celebrations in Bengaluru, 36 deaths at a political rally in Tamil Nadu and 121 deaths at a Hindu gathering in Uttar Pradesh in 2024. The page text did not say whether an inquiry into the Kolkata incident has been announced.

Kenya's Ministry of Health said on Saturday that four more people have tested positive for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, bringing the country's confirmed total to seven, according to Al Jazeera. Three of the new cases are health workers who treated Kenya's first patient. The fourth is a relative of that patient, who died of the disease and had been in quarantine since October 6.

The new cases come a day after Kenya confirmed three cases. The patient identified on Friday was described as a primary contact and close relative of the first and second cases. The index patient had been ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo for a month, flew to Nairobi on October 3 and died on October 5. The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya.

The ministry said 128 of the first patient's 130 contacts, or 98.5 percent, had been quarantined, above the global benchmark of 85 percent needed to break the chain of transmission. It said it has traced and quarantined nearly all of those contacts and that there is no evidence of spread in the community. Kenya has strengthened screening and set up a hotline. Al Jazeera noted that some observers have questioned how the index patient bypassed health screenings and met so many people.

Kenya's cases are linked to the epidemic in the DRC, which has recorded more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May. The dominant strain is Bundibugyo, for which there are currently no vaccines or treatments, which has complicated control efforts. Research is under way on vaccines, and some are in early human testing.

The Norte Fire, a fast-moving wildfire in Orange County, California, has burned six homes, according to The Guardian and the BBC. It started on Friday in San Clemente and was driven by wind into San Juan Capistrano. By Saturday morning it had spread to 570 acres and was 5 percent contained, officials said.

The Guardian reported that about 6,000 homes, with 16,000 residents, were under mandatory evacuation, and that a shelter had opened in each city. The Orange County Fire Authority said the cause is under investigation. Chief TJ McGovern said there were no reports of resident injuries or deaths, and that the fire moved fast because of weather and topography. The Guardian reported two firefighters were taken to hospital with heat-related injuries, while the BBC, citing a Friday evening update, reported one firefighter with heat exhaustion.

Gusts ranged from 50 to 70 mph, according to The Guardian. The National Weather Service said the Santa Ana winds would linger through Saturday, and that the potential for extreme fire behavior could still rise. A red flag warning for parts of southern California was in effect through Saturday night. The BBC said temperatures were far above average and were forecast to reach 95F in southern California on Saturday.

The BBC, citing the state fire agency, said Norte is one of 10 fires burning in California. The Henderson Fire in San Diego County had burned more than 3,100 acres and was about 35 percent contained, and the BBC said it twice forced closures of Interstate 5. The BBC also reported that the Bryson Fire in Malibu had grown to 147 acres and was 52 percent contained. The Guardian said utilities in northern California had cut power to nearly 62,000 customers to help prevent new fires.

A federal immigration officer who struck a Houston construction worker with a vehicle on October 10 was apparently pursuing a man who died years ago, according to the dead man's family and an advocacy group, as reported by The Guardian. The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to the group FIEL.

ICE said in a statement that officers saw their target, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, get into a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. A spokesperson for the Harris County district attorney's office told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle. FIEL says the photo ICE released of its target actually shows Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he tried to re-enter the US. His daughter provided a Mexican death certificate, which has been given to the district attorney, according to FIEL. Her husband confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was her late father. ICE and Customs and Border Protection did not respond to requests for comment.

District Attorney Sean Teare is considering criminal charges against the officer who drove. He has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE's claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle. The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median toward a man running away, and then shows him on the ground, though the impact itself is blocked from view.

FIEL's executive director, Cesar Espinosa, accused ICE of lying. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, a Houston Democrat, said it raises serious questions about whether agents verify who they are looking for. FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez's release before he is moved from hospital to a federal detention center. The sister of another man held in the ICE vehicle asked that he be released so he could serve as a witness.

TikTok has permanently banned the advertising account for "Musk," Alex Gibney's four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, according to The Verge and TechCrunch, both citing The Hollywood Reporter. The film's distributor, Bleecker Street, was told on Friday afternoon of a "permanent suspension." TechCrunch reported the suspension was attributed to the account's political content. TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment from either outlet, and Bleecker Street had not yet responded to The Verge.

The ban follows earlier trouble with advertising. Last month, ads for the film were rejected by YouTube, Meta, X and TikTok. YouTube and Google reversed course, calling the rejection an "error," and Meta also blamed an error and allowed the ad. TikTok and X have not changed their positions, and neither platform has allowed paid advertisements for the film. X is owned by Musk.

The Verge noted that TikTok has no official affiliation with Musk, but that part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film through a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase. TechCrunch reported that Ellison's ownership stake is in TikTok's U.S. operations, and that he and Musk have both been notable supporters of President Donald Trump. The Verge said that shortly before it was removed, the account posted that people should see the movie "before it gets shut down."

"Musk" opened in four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more widely. TechCrunch reported that Gibney confirmed the international distributor, Universal, had wavered on releasing it but is now moving forward. The film is supposed to stream on HBO next year; HBO is now part of Paramount/Skydance, which is led by Ellison's son David.

Israeli drone attacks killed at least six Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Saturday, according to Palestinian medical and emergency workers cited by Al Jazeera. The strikes hit northern, central and southern Gaza, a year after a United States-brokered ceasefire was announced on October 10, 2025.

Palestinian news agency Wafa and hospital staff described the incidents. One man was killed and several wounded when a drone struck civilians near al-Faluja cemetery, west of Jabalia. Another person died in al-Mawasi in Rafah. Two people were killed in the Tuffah neighbourhood of northeast Gaza City, where witnesses told Al Jazeera the victims were returning from the burial of an earlier attack victim. One person was killed in eastern Gaza City and one in Deir el-Balah. The Israeli response to these specific strikes was not included in the page text.

Gaza's Health Ministry said 1,511 Palestinians have been killed and 5,375 injured since the ceasefire was announced. It put the toll since the war began in October 2023 at 74,469 killed and 175,492 injured. UNICEF spokesman Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva on Friday that more than 340 children had been killed since the ceasefire began. He said seven children died in attacks over the previous two weeks and at least 33 were seriously injured, and that about 800,000 children remain displaced, many in tents or unsafe buildings as winter approaches.

Al Jazeera also reported on conditions on the ground. Its mapping published on October 12 showed Israeli forces control or restrict access to about 65 percent of the territory, with the "Yellow Line" pushed further into Palestinian areas. The remaining accessible area is home to 2.1 million people. The Health Ministry warned that more than 1.4 million people face crisis-level food insecurity or worse for the rest of the year.
